items.stem: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury develops a sudden pounding headache, flushing above the injury, and blood pressure 210/110 mm Hg. A urinary catheter has not drained for several hours. Which nursing actions are the priority?

options.text: Elevate the head of the bed, loosen restrictive clothing, and check/relieve bladder distention while notifying the provider.
Lay the client flat and encourage a large oral fluid bolus to raise blood pressure further.
Ignore the headache and wait for blood pressure to normalize without assessing the catheter.
Apply abdominal binders tightly and clamp the catheter for 2 hours.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states provocative stimuli (commonly bladder distention/blocked catheter) must be corrected/removed and severe hypertension treated. WTCS Open RN directs elevating the head of the bed, loosening restrictive clothing, and emptying bowel/bladder to remove the trigger.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Flat positioning and further volume loading worsen hypertensive emergency; WTCS advises elevating the head/sitting to help reduce blood pressure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Autonomic dysreflexia is a medical emergency; both sources require removing the trigger and addressing hypertension promptly.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Tight binders and clamping a catheter can worsen bladder/abdominal stimuli that provoke dysreflexia.

items.stem: An adult has continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for 8 minutes without return of consciousness. Complete the bowtie: identify the priority condition, two nursing actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Isolated uncomplicated migraine without seizure activity
Stable well-controlled absence seizures lasting under 30 seconds
Benign essential tremor without impaired awareness

actions.text: Support airway/breathing (position for airway protection; prepare for advanced airway if compromise)
Obtain IV access and administer an ordered intravenous benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam) promptly
Force a padded tongue blade between the teeth during the seizure
Delay antiseizure medication until the seizure has lasted 60 minutes
Leave the client alone in a locked room without monitoring

parameters.text: Respiratory status and signs of airway compromise
Seizure activity duration and return of consciousness

rationales.K1: Correct. Merck defines generalized convulsive status epilepticus as tonic-clonic activity lasting >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness.
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Migraine alone does not meet status epilepticus criteria.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Brief controlled absence seizures are not status epilepticus.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Essential tremor is not continuous seizure activity.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck requires monitoring respiratory status and intubation if airway compromise; OpenStax directs side-lying airway protection during seizure care.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck: give IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam/midazolam/diazepam) promptly for seizures lasting >5 minutes; OpenStax states IV lorazepam or midazolam is used to treat status epilepticus.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. OpenStax: never place fingers or barriers between the teeth during a seizure.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Merck emphasizes earlier treatment improves control; waiting 60 minutes risks brain injury.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Continuous monitoring and emergency treatment are required.
rationales.P1: Correct. Merck highlights respiratory/airway monitoring during status treatment.
rationales.P2: Correct. Duration and recovery of consciousness define status and response to therapy (Merck).
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Unrelated to acute neurologic emergency monitoring.

items.stem: A construction worker collapses on a hot day with confusion, hot skin, and a rectal temperature of 41.2 °C (106.2 °F). Which action is the priority while emergency services are activated?

options.text: Begin rapid cooling immediately (e.g., cool/cold-water immersion or evaporative cooling with wet skin and fanning) and do not delay for hospital arrival.
Wrap the client in heavy blankets to conserve heat until the fever breaks spontaneously.
Offer alcoholic beverages to promote vasodilation and wait outdoors in direct sun.
Avoid any cooling measures until laboratory results return from the hospital.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck emphasizes rapid recognition and aggressive cooling as the initial treatment goal. CDC Yellow Book states not to delay cooling—use immersion or evaporative methods and activate emergency care.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Heatstroke requires heat removal, not heat conservation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Alcohol and continued heat exposure worsen injury; cooling and shade/removal from heat are required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Both sources prioritize immediate cooling; waiting for labs delays definitive first aid.

items.stem: A healthy 62-year-old client asks about preventing shingles. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Recombinant zoster (shingles) vaccine is recommended for adults 50 years and older as a two-dose series.
Shingles vaccination is unnecessary after age 50 because risk falls with aging.
Only infants receive shingles vaccine as part of the routine childhood schedule.
A single childhood varicella dose fully replaces adult shingles vaccination for life.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC recommends shingles vaccine for adults ≥50 (2 doses). Merck likewise indicates recombinant zoster vaccine for adults ≥50 years.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources note risk rises with age and recommend vaccination at ≥50.
rationales.C: Incorrect. This is an adult immunization indication, not a routine infant vaccine.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Prior varicella history/vaccine does not replace adult recombinant zoster vaccination per CDC/Merck.

items.stem: A public health nurse counsels parents of a healthy 6-month-old about pneumococcal disease prevention. Which statement is appropriate?

options.text: Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for all children younger than 5 years of age.
Pneumococcal vaccines are only for adults and never given in childhood.
Healthy infants should avoid all pneumococcal vaccines until age 18.
Pneumococcal vaccination is useful only after meningitis has already occurred.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all children younger than 5 years. Merck states children up to 18 years should receive pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15 or PCV20).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources include routine pediatric indications.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Delaying until adulthood contradicts childhood schedule recommendations.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Vaccination is primary prevention before invasive disease.

items.stem: A client who recently started haloperidol develops high fever, lead-pipe muscle rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic (causative medication) and initiate emergency supportive care including rapid cooling as indicated.
Double the haloperidol dose to overcome rigidity.
Encourage vigorous outdoor exercise in hot weather to 'work off' the rigidity.
Document findings only and reassess in 48 hours without notifying the provider.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck treatment begins with discontinuation of the causative medication plus aggressive supportive care and rapid cooling. OpenStax describes NMS as a medical emergency requiring removal of the offending agent, cooling, and supportive management.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Continuing/escalating the dopamine-blocking drug worsens NMS; both sources require stopping it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Exertion/heat exposure aggravates hyperthermia; cooling is required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Delay risks fatal complications; urgent recognition and treatment are required.

items.stem: Complete the nursing teaching about neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) risk with antipsychotics.

ngn.template: NMS is a medical emergency featuring altered mentation, severe muscle rigidity, and {B1}. The priority medication action is to {B2}.

B1.text: hyperthermia with autonomic instability (e.g., tachycardia, labile blood pressure)
isolated mild nail ridging without systemic signs
improved sleep with no vital-sign changes

B2.text: stop the causative antipsychotic and provide urgent supportive care/cooling
switch to a higher-potency depot injection without assessment
withhold all fluids for 24 hours routinely

rationales.B1a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax list altered mental status, rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic hyperactivity as NMS features.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Nail ridging alone is not an NMS defining cluster.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Hair growth is unrelated to NMS recognition.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. NMS includes fever and autonomic instability, not stable vitals only.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Merck: discontinue causative medication and cool/support. OpenStax: remove offending agent and institute supportive cooling care.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Dose escalation of the offending agent is contraindicated.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Continuing dopamine blockade can worsen NMS.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Supportive care includes managing fluids/electrolytes, not routine total fluid withholding.

items.stem: A euvolemic client with SIADH has serum sodium 128 mmol/L and is alert. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate based on the primary treatment approach?

options.text: Implement the prescribed fluid (water) restriction and monitor intake, output, and daily weight.
Encourage free water intake of several litres daily to dilute sodium further.
Stop all sodium monitoring because SIADH never affects neurologic status.
Replace free water with unrestricted hypotonic fluids without an order.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck lists fluid restriction as primary SIADH treatment. OpenStax emphasizes fluid restriction with intake/output and daily weights to limit further water accumulation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Excess free water worsens dilutional hyponatremia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Both sources link falling sodium to neurologic risk (seizures/coma).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unordered hypotonic free-water loads contradict restriction therapy.

items.stem: After blunt chest trauma, a client develops hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and neck-vein distention. Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?

options.text: Suspect cardiac tamponade and prepare for emergent pericardial drainage (pericardiocentesis/surgical decompression) while activating the emergency response.
Assume dehydration only and encourage ambulation without cardiac assessment.
Interpret muffled sounds as reassuring and delay notification of the provider.
Place the client in Trendelenburg and withhold all further evaluation.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck describes Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled tones, venous distention) and treats tamponade with immediate pericardiocentesis/pericardiotomy. OpenStax explains pericardial fluid impairs filling and requires drainage.
rationales.B: Incorrect. This triad after trauma suggests obstructive tamponade, not simple dehydration ambulatory care.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Muffled sounds are a classic tamponade cue requiring urgent action (Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Emergent decompression planning and evaluation are required, not delayed positioning-only care.

items.stem: A medication order is missing the dose and the writing is unclear. What should the nurse do before administering the drug?

options.text: Contact the prescriber to clarify and correct the incomplete/unclear order, and do not give the medication until it is clarified.
Guess a usual adult dose from memory and administer immediately.
Ask another client what dose they take at home and use that amount.
Omit documentation of the unclear order and proceed quietly.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: if any order component is missing or unclear, contact the prescriber to clarify and correct before administration. OpenStax Fundamentals: communicate clearly to the provider when orders appear inappropriate or inaccurate and document.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Guessing doses violates rights of medication administration and safe verification.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Another client's home dose is not a valid order for this client.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Failure to clarify and document increases risk and liability.

items.stem: A client with cervical spinal cord injury shows sudden hypertension and severe headache concerning for autonomic dysreflexia. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated now.

rows.text: Elevate the head of the bed / assist to a sitting position if safe.
Loosen restrictive clothing and assess for bladder distention or blocked catheter.
Lay the client completely flat and clamp the urinary catheter for several hours.
Notify the provider/rapid response and continue blood pressure monitoring.

rationales.R1: Indicated. WTCS: elevate HOB/sitting position to help reduce blood pressure during autonomic dysreflexia.
rationales.R2: Indicated. WTCS and Merck: remove triggers such as restrictive clothing and bladder distention/blocked catheter.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Flat positioning and clamping a catheter can worsen the hypertensive crisis and bladder stimulus.
rationales.R4: Indicated. Merck requires close vital-sign monitoring and management of severe hypertension; notify for urgent treatment.

items.stem: A client reports tingling and progressive bilateral leg weakness that is now ascending toward the arms after a recent gastrointestinal infection. Which assessment finding is the highest priority to monitor closely?

options.text: Respiratory effort and signs of ventilatory failure (because paralysis can involve respiratory muscles).
Preference for morning versus evening television programming.
Ability to rearrange bedside flowers independently as the only outcome measure.
Hair length and styling choices during hospitalization.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck notes weakness often begins in the legs and progresses, and respiratory paralysis may require mechanical ventilation. WTCS states weakness can progress to paralysis and GBS can be fatal if respiratory muscles are affected.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Entertainment preference is unrelated to life-threatening ventilatory risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Functional hobbies do not replace respiratory monitoring priority.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Cosmetic concerns are not the priority assessment in ascending paralysis.
